newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM dismisses devaluation idea - paper.
newsitem.headline: Czech PM dismisses devaluation idea - paper.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, while preparing a package of new economic measures to be announced next week, has again dismissed the idea that a devaluation of the crown might be one of the steps, the daily Hospodarske Noviny reported on Friday.
"The word devaluation itself is not a topic that would worry me right now," the paper quoted Klaus as saying during a party meeting on Thursday in the town of Trebic.

Officials including Klaus and Czech National Bank (CNB) governor Josef Tosovsky have repeatedly said a devaluation is not part of the measures they would consider to stem a massive foreign trade deficit, which has driven the current account deficit over eight percent of gross domestic product.

But markets have been increasingly nervous awaiting the outcome of an April 16 cabinet meeting which is supposed to decide on measures to cut the foreign trade deficit, stimulate the economy, cut wage growth and bring state finances to a balance.
Hospodarske Noviny quoted the prime minister as saying that a solution to the foreign trade gap had not been found yet.

Klaus has also dismissed imposing an import surcharge, an idea sponsored by Agriculture Minister Josef Lux, saying it could only be imposed by a law approved by parliament, and thus was unrealistic to consider in the short-term.

The CNB on Thursday lowered minimum reserve requirements for commercial banks to 9.5 percent from 11.5 percent, hoping to give some slack to banks to lend in an economy which slowed to lower-than-expected 4.4 percent growth in 1996.
Klaus and other cabinet ministers have called on the central bank to relax its restrictive monetary policy.
